templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Emphasis: stronger same-direction fact (content-contrast trap at hard)
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: In his 1499 treatise The Judgment of Two Languages, Central Asian poet Alisher Navoi maintained that Chagatai Turkic, his native language, was a richer medium for poetry than Persian, then the region’s dominant literary language. ______ Navoi himself composed considerable verse in Persian, under the pen name Fani. But the overwhelming majority of his writing is in Turkic.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says Navoi championed Turkic as a language for poetry. The blank sentence admits a fact that seems to cut against that: he also wrote poems in Persian. The next sentence turns back with “But”: most of his work is in Turkic. “Granted” introduces a point the writer concedes before returning to the main claim.

A.why_wrong: Arguing that Turkic suited poetry would not cause Navoi to write verse in Persian; the Persian poems are a point against the argument, not a result of it.

C.why_wrong: “Additionally” would present the Persian verse as one more point supporting Navoi’s case for Turkic, but writing in Persian seems to work against that case, which is why the next sentence begins with “But.”

D.why_wrong: Writing verse in Persian is not similar to arguing for Turkic; it is a concession that the following sentence answers.

items.notes: Grant then turn, the turn in the next sentence opened by But (3.19 shape, with But for Still). K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so this is a strong band 6: rare key, the turn a sentence after the blank, no contrast or emphasis decoy (no In fact beside the concession key). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

fixes: passage: Navoi's thesis sharpened from 'every bit as expressive a medium for poetry as Persian' to 'a richer medium for poetry than Persian' (the treatise argues Turkic's superiority), which also makes the grant cleaner; 'the dominant literary language of Central Asia' to 'then the region’s dominant literary language' (Central Asian ... Central Asia repeated); 62 to 58 words

Second-sense check: no In fact or Indeed beside the concession key; Additionally and Similarly are CB's own decoys beside a grant (f5959727: Furthermore, Similarly); Similarly: no matching case named.

items.passage: Gyotaku, a printmaking technique that originated in nineteenth-century Japan, gave anglers an exact record of their catches. Because each print is pulled directly from an inked fish, it preserves the animal’s true size and the precise arrangement of its scales and fins. ______ the eye, which rarely prints clearly, is typically painted in by hand afterward.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences claim that a gyotaku print is an exact record because it comes straight from the fish. The blank sentence admits a limit to that claim: one part, the eye, is not printed at all but painted in by hand. “Admittedly” introduces a fact that qualifies the claim without overturning it.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the claim that the print is an exact record; it points out a part of the print that is added by hand.

B.why_wrong: “Furthermore” would add another point in support of the print’s accuracy, but an eye painted in by hand is a limit on that accuracy.

C.why_wrong: The eye is not one of the details the print preserves exactly; it is the one detail the print fails to capture, so the sentence does not specify the earlier claim.

items.notes: Supported claim, then the one detail that qualifies it (3.14 shape: a property that holds except under one condition). Key Admittedly, new for K2 in our bank (That said x4 and Granted x1 so far). No In fact or Indeed on offer (second-sense rule). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

review.notes: No fact check (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation: named people and institutions are real and carry their commonly reported facts, researchers behind findings are unnamed. Second-sense check: no In fact or Indeed beside the qualification key; Specifically fails because the eye is the one detail the print does not capture.

items.passage: Early modern Europeans are often imagined to have married in their early teens. Demographers analyzing parish registers, which recorded local baptisms, marriages, and burials, have found little evidence supporting that image; ______ in England and much of northwestern Europe between the 1500s and the 1700s, women typically first married not as teenagers but in their mid-twenties.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first clause of the second sentence says that demographers found little evidence for the image of very early marriage. The clause after the blank gives the exact finding: women usually first married not as teenagers but in their mid-twenties. “Specifically” signals that this clause spells out what the demographers found.

B.why_wrong: The clause after the blank agrees with the clause before it: marriage in the mid-twenties is the evidence that fails to support the image of teenage marriage. It contrasts only with the popular image in the first sentence, not with the demographers’ finding.

C.why_wrong: The typical marriage ages are not a result of the demographers finding little support for the image; they are the evidence behind that finding.

D.why_wrong: The clause after the blank is not a separate point added to the demographers’ conclusion; it is the content of that conclusion.

items.notes: Band-7 S1 (d3b7d7a3 move): a popular account, then researchers who undercut it, then after a semicolon the exact finding, which contradicts the first sentence so that nonetheless pulls. Varied from w1b1_03 (in many cases, with an interrupter) and w1b3_02 (More often, explicit share): no interrupter, no quantity, and a specification key rather than a frequency key. Decoy trio differs from the model’s (for this reason, additionally, nevertheless). No in fact or indeed on offer (in fact would fit as a correction). Hajnal’s European marriage pattern (women about 25 to 26, men about 27 to 28 in early modern England). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.
band7_moves: surface contrast: the clause after the blank contradicts the popular image in sentence 1, so nonetheless reads right on a first pass
key outside the core 13 (specifically); the clause it introduces repeats none of the wording before the blank
each decoy is a common connective with a plausible misreading (separate point, consequence, despite); no sequence or summary decoy
blank after a semicolon, lowercase options

review.notes: No fact check (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation: named people and institutions are real and carry their commonly reported facts, researchers behind findings are unnamed. Second-sense check: no in fact or indeed on offer (in fact would fit as a correction); nonetheless dies on the clause before the blank, thus on direction, in addition because 'not as teenagers but' ties the clause to the finding.

band7.why: Specification form: specifically spells out a general finding, the frame of the band-6 S1 item 8e9677e6, not the frequency key of the band-7 model d3b7d7a3. The surface contrast ('not as teenagers but' against sentence 1) is already resolved by the clause right before the blank ('little evidence supporting that image'), and the one band-6 S1 item with surface contrast (4b7a84b0) shows that trap alone does not lift this frame. Register 5.20 fails gate 4; the combined gate passes via proxy 3. Not hardened: the frequency frame is already used by w1b1_03 and w1b3_02, and dropping 'not as teenagers but' would let in addition read as a second finding. band_target left at 7 as in w1b3_02.

items.passage: Chinese artist Xu Bing’s installation Book from the Sky (1987–1991) fills a gallery with hand-printed volumes and suspended scrolls covered in what appear to be Chinese characters. Viewers who read Chinese, however, find the text entirely illegible. ______ all of the roughly 4,000 characters are Xu’s own inventions: none appears in any Chinese dictionary.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that even fluent readers of Chinese cannot read the work. The blank sentence backs that up with a stronger fact: every one of the characters is invented, so none of them could be read. “Indeed” signals that the sentence confirms and strengthens the previous point.

A.why_wrong: The invented characters do not hold true in spite of the work being unreadable; they are the reason it is unreadable, so the two sentences point the same way.

B.why_wrong: Xu did not invent the characters because viewers could not read the work; the reverse is true, since the invented characters are what make it unreadable.

D.why_wrong: The sentence does not describe a second, similar case; it adds force to the same point about the work’s unreadability.

items.notes: Plain band-6 emphasis: a claim (unreadable), then the stronger fact behind it. The however in sentence 2 primes a contrast so that Nevertheless pulls; not the outlier-then-majority frame of the band-7 models or of w1b1_05. No To that end or For example on offer (Xu’s intent and an example reading would both be arguable). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Japanese architect Tadao Ando is renowned for buildings of exposed concrete, their smooth gray surfaces left unadorned inside and out in churches, museums, and residences alike. ______ for Japan’s pavilion at the 1992 world’s fair in Spain, he designed an enormous hall framed in timber, its tiers of interlocking wooden brackets recalling the joinery of traditional Japanese temples.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes Ando’s usual material, bare concrete. The blank sentence describes a building that departs from that habit: a hall framed in timber, chosen to echo traditional Japanese temples. “Nonetheless” signals that this project is an exception to what the first sentence would lead the reader to expect.

A.why_wrong: Ando’s reputation for concrete does not lead to a timber building; the pavilion goes against that reputation rather than following from it.

B.why_wrong: The pavilion is not a particular case of Ando’s concrete buildings; it is built of wood, so it is an exception to the habit, not a detail of it.

C.why_wrong: A timber hall is not like the concrete buildings described in the first sentence; it differs from them.

items.notes: Band-7 C3 (fc95a352 move): a habit, then a one-off exception with a purpose (timber to recall temple joinery), keyed with a concession word in its exception role and no other adversative option. Varied from w1b3_04 (Nevertheless, rail gauge): key Nonetheless, a named building rather than a named line, and a new decoy trio (Accordingly, In particular, Likewise). Seville is not named (already a Transitions subject). Japan Pavilion, Expo ’92, one of the largest timber buildings of its day with bracket tiers after temple construction. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

The material cue (timber) is the 18th word after the blank, so a reader who stops at the named pavilion picks In particular. items.passage: A standard violin has four strings, each bowed or plucked by the performer. The Hardanger fiddle of western Norway, ______ typically has eight or nine: four conventional playing strings and four or five additional strings positioned beneath the fingerboard, which resonate sympathetically when the others are bowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the number of strings on a standard violin (four). The second gives the number on the Hardanger fiddle (eight or nine). “By comparison” signals that the second instrument is being measured against the first on the same feature.

B.why_wrong: The Hardanger fiddle is not an example of a standard four-string violin; it has twice as many strings.

C.why_wrong: “Likewise” would say the Hardanger fiddle is like the standard violin, but it differs from it in the very feature described.

D.why_wrong: The number of strings on a standard violin does not cause the Hardanger fiddle to have eight or nine.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute, numbers (By comparison is CB’s choice for a numeric contrast, 1.14), placed as an interrupter after the subject (2.6). items.passage: The Moon’s gravity gradually slows Earth’s rotation, so days steadily lengthen. Hundreds of millions of years ago, they were considerably shorter than they are today. ______ each year, the time Earth takes to orbit the Sun, contained more days: growth lines in fossil corals about 380 million years old suggest approximately 400.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences explain that the Moon slows Earth’s rotation, so days were shorter long ago. The blank sentence draws the conclusion that follows: if each day was shorter, a year must have held more of them. “Thus” signals that the sentence follows from the one before it.

A.why_wrong: A year holding more days does not contrast with days being shorter; it follows from it.

C.why_wrong: “Regardless” would mean the number of days in a year has nothing to do with the length of a day, but it depends directly on it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing is being listed, so there is no first point for “Firstly” to introduce.

items.notes: Principle, then what follows from it (1.32 kind). items.passage: Many flowers bear markings that are invisible to humans but conspicuous to bees, which can perceive ultraviolet light. ______ the petals of the black-eyed Susan look uniformly yellow to people, but under ultraviolet light the base of each petal appears dark, forming a bull’s-eye that may guide bees toward the flower’s nectar.

items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: many flowers have markings that bees can see but people cannot. The blank sentence gives one specific flower with such a marking, the black-eyed Susan. “For example” signals that the sentence offers an instance of the general claim.

A.why_wrong: The black-eyed Susan does not contrast with the general claim; it is a case of it.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does not sum up the text; it introduces a specific new case.

C.why_wrong: The sentence describes how the flower looks now, not something that happened before the claim in the first sentence.

items.passage: Volapük, a language invented in 1879 by German priest Johann Martin Schleyer, spread rapidly across Europe. Within a decade it had attracted thousands of enthusiasts, and its 1889 congress in Paris was conducted entirely in Volapük. ______ the movement soon collapsed, as many adherents abandoned it for simpler invented languages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe Volapük’s quick success. The blank sentence describes its sudden decline. “However” signals that this sentence contrasts with the success just described.

A.why_wrong: The language’s quick spread did not cause its collapse; the collapse came because followers left for easier languages.

B.why_wrong: The collapse of the movement is not a rewording of its success; it is the opposite.

items.passage: Farming in ancient Egypt depended on the Nile’s yearly flood: a low flood left fields parched, while an unusually high one could destroy villages. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that officials needed to predict each year’s harvest, which depended on the flood. The blank sentence gives the action they took to meet that need: building nilometers to measure the river’s rise. “Therefore” signals that the action follows from the need.

B.why_wrong: Building nilometers is not similar to needing to anticipate the harvest; it is the response to that need.

C.why_wrong: Building nilometers does not go against the officials’ need; it serves it.

items.passage: Russian painter Igor Savitsky sought to preserve the work of Soviet avant-garde artists, whose experimental styles had been officially condemned. ______ beginning in the 1960s, he acquired thousands of their paintings, often from the artists’ families, for a museum he established in Nukus, a remote city in what is now Uzbekistan.

items.explanation: The first sentence states Savitsky’s goal: to save works by condemned avant-garde artists. The blank sentence describes what he did to reach that goal: he bought thousands of their works for his museum. “To that end” signals an action taken to achieve the goal just stated.
